name: Rafael Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, separate from employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tend a coil-winding machine that winds copper wire for small electric motors. I thread the spool, watch the tension and count damaged windings before the coils go to assembly. I joined after a warehouse job and am still the junior operator at 58, learning how different wire gauges behave. I finished secondary school and earn an ordinary machine-operator wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you deal with new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mariam works at a community kitchen, and our grown sons live on their own. We rent and have about three months of expenses saved; there are some similar plants near us. I use AI every day to explain diagrams and put my shift notes in order, then check any winding setting with the printed sheet and a trainer. I like trying a new tool early, but I keep a hand away from a moving spindle until somebody shows me a safe stop. We talk about retirement, though no amount is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the winding crew that better office software might tidy orders, but the copper still has to be wound at the right tension. I would offer to help explain any new screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present two wages pay the rent and three months saved covers a short interruption. I am junior on the winder but learning fast. A slow change gives me time to improve the physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking wire tension with the trainer at the first spool. I would use AI to draft a clearer shift note, then verify the turn count from the printed specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel reasonably calm about the line continuing. My weak point is experience, so more ordinary practice helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a new operator notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A spool can look neat until a damaged turn catches under the next layer. I slow the copper winder and check the wire tension before another motor coil is wasted. The trainer showed me that last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI set the winder speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from a phone answer. I ask AI to explain the terms, then use the printed range and the trainer’s check for the actual setting. I can be curious without gambling a run.

say: I would **help** explain new order screens while keeping physical tension checks.
The **printed** winding specification still sets the machine.
think: **Two** wages cover rent and three months saved gives short breathing room.
I **am** a junior winder but learning quickly.
do: **Keep** checking first-spool tension with the trainer.
**Use** AI for clearer notes while verifying turn counts against printed specifications.
feel: **Reasonably** calm about continued work and practice on the line.
S0.quote: I slow the copper winder and check the wire tension before another motor coil is wasted.
fieldNote: **Rafael** is a junior copper-coil machine operator still learning wire gauges and spindle checks.
He **uses** AI daily for diagrams and notes but verifies settings against printed instructions and a trainer.
**Three** months saved and ordinary household wages make a slow change manageable, though he still needs experience.

steps.text: Keep checking first-spool tension with trainer and printed specifications

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew office software can change plans before a robot begins loading coils. I would ask for a safe pilot on our machine and for the union branch to see any proposed roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot loader might cut packing and operator hours later; I am still new enough to be exposed. Three months saved will not carry many months of rent. I can pick up a new interface quickly, but only a real shift plan shows whether that helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an offered paid lesson on the new AI planning screen and compare its coil list with our paper order. I would attend the union meeting about paid robot instruction and staffing. If a local coil-checking vacancy is posted, I would apply only if its net pay after travel and shift cover rent and household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about hours but keen to see what a tested tool can do. I would not operate a robot arm from watching a demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot pilot include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guarded full shift, a fitter explaining how to stop the arm, and damaged-coil counts beside our old numbers. I would ask to observe first. Actual control practice needs an offered paid supervised place with isolation checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the checking vacancy never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current wage and search posted coil or packing jobs at the other nearby plants. Each application needs a real vacancy, a wage after travel that pays rent and a shift Mariam and I can manage. I would not leave on a promise.

say: I would **ask** for a guarded pilot and union review of roster plans.
**Office** planning software arrives before physical coil loading.
think: A **later** coil-loading robot may cut my junior winding hours.
**Three** months saved cannot carry a long rent gap.
do: **Learn** offered AI planning screen on paid time and verify paper orders.
**Attend** union meeting on robot training and staffing.
**Apply** for posted coil-checking work only with rent-covering net pay and shift.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, curious about tested tools and safe instruction.
S1.quote: I would not operate a robot arm from watching a demo.
fieldNote: **Rafael** would actually learn a new AI planning screen only through offered paid instruction and paper-order checks.
He **attends** a union meeting about staffing, while robot operation needs a separate offered supervised safety place.
A **posted** checking role must offer adequate net pay and shift; a no-vacancy search checks other actual nearby postings.

steps.text: Learn offered AI planning screen on paid time with paper-order checks
Attend union branch meeting about robot instruction and roster
Apply for posted coil-checking role only with rent-covering net pay and shift
Search posted local coil jobs if no checking vacancy and pay and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union branch that AGI can handle orders in 2028, but capable robots loading, winding and checking coils around 2031 could change the whole floor. We need written paid-training and job terms now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut to junior winding shifts if robots can run the spindles and check each coil. I will be 63 then, with only three months saved. Mariam’s kitchen hours may not be enough if mine disappear, and I would wake at night working out the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned holiday and list rent, power and food costs. I would ask the union branch to seek written redeployment terms and ask the landlord about a payment arrangement before missing rent. I would apply for a posted local electrical inspection job only if the employer offers paid supervised safety training and its net pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the expected wage loss. I can make a plan for lost coil shifts, but three months of savings is not an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your quick learning keep you employed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might help if a real safe job opens, but no screen skill qualifies me to reach into a robot spindle. I would need paid supervised isolation practice. I would not count on being chosen without a posted role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons pay the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not make that their job. They have separate households. If one offers help, I would count only the amount actually offered, after we have asked for written work and rent terms.

say: I would **seek** written terms before capable coil robots around 2031.
**AGI** changes orders in 2028, about three years earlier.
think: **Three** months saved cannot replace my wage while partner hours are uncertain.
do: **Ask** union for redeployment terms and landlord about rent timing.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with paid safety instruction and bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless over rent.
S2.quote: I can make a plan for lost coil shifts, but three months of savings is not an income.
fieldNote: **Rafael** expects capable hands-on robots to threaten winding shifts around 2031, after AGI changes orders.
**Despite** curiosity, he recognises that a screen skill is not robot-isolation competence.
**Inspection** requires an actual posting, paid supervised safety training and wages and hours that cover rent.

steps.text: Cancel planned holiday and list rent power and food bills
Ask union branch for written redeployment terms
Ask landlord about payment arrangement before missing rent
Apply for posted inspection role only with paid safe training bill-covering net pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that five years should produce real course places for junior workers, not only a brochure for experienced fitters. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable winding robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 near that robot date. I can learn a new interface quickly, but safe electrical and mechanical isolation is another skill. Three months saved gives a little room; it does not make retirement possible without real income figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in an offered recognised coil-inspection course only if it is funded, pays for class hours, includes supervised robot and electrical isolation and fits the shifts I work. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection role only if net pay after travel and hours cover our rent. If no paid place opens, I would remain on the winder and check posted local operator jobs with sufficient pay and usable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about course and job availability, but interested in learning the real controls. A paid practical place would give me a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI be part of your study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I would use it to turn a wiring diagram into questions for the trainer, then test the printed diagram against the machine. I would not let a chatbot certify a dead circuit. The fitter must watch me isolate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 66 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Mariam and I can see written retirement-income estimates that cover rent, food and care costs. We have not established that. Until then I would need a paid role, not a birthday rule.

say: I would **ask** for recognised paid practical places for junior operators.
2031 **order** changes precede capable winding robots around 2034.
think: At 66, **quick** screen learning does not prove robot isolation skill.
**Three** months saved does not establish retirement income.
do: **Enrol** in offered funded paid course with supervised robot electrical isolation and workable shifts.
**Apply** after qualifying for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay and hours.
If **no** paid course, seek posted operator work with sufficient pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about place availability, interested in practical safe learning.
S3.quote: I would not let a chatbot certify a dead circuit.
fieldNote: **Rafael** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot and electrical isolation on workable shifts.
**After** training he applies separately for a posted job whose net pay and hours cover rent.
**Without** a paid place he keeps the winder wage while checking posted local operator work.

steps.text: Enrol in offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot isolation and shifts
Apply after qualification for posted inspection role only with rent-covering net pay and hours
Seek posted local operator work if no course and pay and hours suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that ten years is time to bargain for older junior workers to get paid training too. AGI changes orders in 2036; capable hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036 and 71 at the robot date. I may have left paid shifts before then if actual retirement income covers rent. If the figures do not work, I will need a safe paid position, and a long notice period alone will not create one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written estimates for retirement income and household costs this year. If paid work remains necessary, I would take an offered recognised funded course on paid workable hours with supervised robot and electrical isolation; after qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection job only if net pay and shifts cover rent and travel. Without a paid course I would search posted operator work at adequate wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about an unknown retirement balance, but I can use a long warning to make real choices. I still need the offers written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach younger workers AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already show a colleague how to turn a diagram into questions for the trainer and check the printout. I would keep doing that while I am on the line. I would never call an AI answer a safety sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the union branch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a proposal for paid older-worker practical places with clear selection rules. I would ask others to put their names behind it at a meeting. A training promise should include the people who are newest on the floor.

say: I would **bring** paid older-worker training criteria to a union meeting.
I would **separate** 2036 orders from physical winding robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **might** have stopped shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039 any continued employment depends on real figures.
do: Request **retirement figures** and ask the union meeting for paid older-worker places with written criteria.
Take offered **recognised funded paid training** only if retirement figures show wages are needed, with supervised isolation and attendable hours.
Apply for **posted local inspection** after qualifying or operator fallback without a course, only with pay and shifts covering rent/travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about uncertain retirement income, willing to plan with actual offers.
S4.quote: I would never call an AI answer a safety sign-off.
fieldNote: **Rafael** does not assume a pension amount or continued work at 71; retirement depends on written figures.
If **wages** are needed, training requires an offered recognised funded paid place with supervised electrical and robot safety.
A **separate** posted inspection role must pay enough after travel; without a course he checks posted operator jobs.

steps.text: Request written retirement cost and income figures
Take offered funded paid supervised course if work needed and hours fit
Apply locally for posted inspection after course or operator fallback without course, with bill-covering net pay/shifts
Ask union meeting for paid older-worker practical places and written selection criteria

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots could cut junior coil-winding shifts around 2031, when we have only three months saved. A funded paid safety place and a posted job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I like useful technology, and I will ask it questions every day. I would never call an AI answer a safety sign-off. A real trainer has to show me when the coil-winding spindle is safe.

headlineQuote: A real trainer has to show me when the coil-winding spindle is safe.
portrait: **Rafael** Mensah, 58, is a junior copper-coil winder with secondary schooling and typical operator pay.
He and **community-kitchen** worker partner Mariam have grown sons, rent and about three months of expenses saved.
He **uses** AI daily for diagrams and notes but checks printed specifications and safe stops with a trainer.
**Curious** and union-minded, he still fears major robot wage loss because few months of savings cannot carry rent.
He would **take** only offered funded paid supervised training and seek posted work with adequate net wages and shifts.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could remove his junior winding shifts while the household has only three months saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised robot training and posted local work with net wages and shifts covering rent.
